etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from French torrent, from Italian torrente, from Latin torrentem, accusative of torrēns (“burning, seething, roaring”), from Latin torrēre (“to parch, scorch”).

definitions.definition: A violent flow, as of water, lava, etc.; a stream suddenly raised and running rapidly, as down a precipice.

quote.citation: 1841 September 28, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, “[Miscellaneous.] Excelsior.”, in Ballads and Other Poems, 2nd edition, Cambridge, Mass.:  […]  John Owen, published 1842, →OCLC, stanza 4, page 130:
quote.text: "Try not the Pass!" the old man said; / "Dark lowers the tempest overhead, / The roaring torrent is deep and wide!" / And loud that clarion voice replied / Excelsior!

quote.citation: 2013 June 29, “High and wet”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8842, page 28:
quote.text: Floods in northern India, mostly in the small state of Uttarakhand, have wrought disaster on an enormous scale. […] Rock-filled torrents smashed vehicles and homes, burying victims under rubble and sludge.

definitions.definition: (figuratively) A large amount or stream of something.

quote.citation: 1906 August, Alfred Noyes, “The Highwayman”, in Poems, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., published October 1906, →OCLC, part 1, stanza I, page 45:
quote.text: The wind was a torrent of darkness among the gusty trees, / The moon was a ghostly galleon tossed upon cloudy seas, / The road was a ribbon of moonlight over the purple moor, / And the highwayman came riding— / Riding—riding— / The highwayman came riding, up to the old inn-door.

quote.citation: 1907, E.M. Forster, The Longest Journey, Part III, XXXI [Uniform ed., p. 278]:
quote.text: On the banks of the grey torrent of life, love is the only flower.

quote.citation: 1981 December 5, Michael Bronski, “Coming (Out) to Opera”, in Gay Community News, volume 9, number 20, page 6:
quote.text: Western civilization has always taught the repression of emotion  […]  The emotional torrents of opera rebel against this.

quote.citation: 2011 December 21, Helen Pidd, “Europeans migrate south as continent drifts deeper into crisis”, in the Guardian:
quote.text: A new stream of migrants is leaving the continent. It threatens to become a torrent if the debt crisis continues to worsen.

definitions.definition: Rolling or rushing in a rapid stream.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book II”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From BitTorrent and the file extension it uses for metadata (.torrent); ultimately from etymology 1, carrying the notion of the flow of information.

definitions.definition: (Internet, file sharing) A set of files obtainable through a peer-to-peer network, especially BitTorrent.
(Internet slang, transitive) To download in a torrent.

quote.citation: 2009, Rick Dakan, Geek Mafia: Black Hat Blues, page 38:
quote.text: They had two thousand CDs burned with Listnin loaded on them, including versions for every major phone OS, and they'd set up a dozen servers in seven different countries for people to torrent the file from.
